title: Opium and cocaine in early New Orleans
summary: Opium was around, cocaine legal; Eugene Dasty put it on sale in his drugstore window.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Well, in his neighborhood, what was hot was opium. Yeah. And people used to run opium. Mm-hmm. But, uh, you know, opium was an elaborate thing to go through, you had to have all the equipment and everything, and most people didn't bother with that. In fact, there wasn't a big thing with drugs in New Orleans in those days. Mm-hmm. Tom Anderson used to run opium.
But, uh, you didn't have many what they call hopheads. Hmm.
But it was readily available too. Oh, it was available, yeah.

If you wanted cocaine, cocaine was, was... No, cocaine was not very well known. Of course it wasn't illegal, you've got to remember. Exactly. Yeah. And I had this photograph of, uh, of Eugene Dasty's drugstore window. Uh-huh. There was a big pile of cocaine in the window. And there's a sale sign on it. Uh-huh. Well I interviewed him when he was 92 years old, confronted him with this photograph. Uh-huh. And I said, it says cocaine sale.
So, I said, how did you get away with this? He said, what? He said, you know, it wasn't illegal, no reason why I shouldn't put it on sale. He said, besides, you know, that stuff is perishable.
Now where was his shop? Where was his shop?
His shop was on Bienville and Marais.
